about.what: Reference labels for the 62 facts of stage 2a on lectures 1, 4 and 16 (the think-budget 16384 run of 2026-11-12, as in pipeline/output/nptel_vr/stage_2a_fact_extraction/fact_maps). Labelled by Fable on 2026-11-12 against the segment transcripts and the eight properties of pipeline/prompts/fact_judge.txt.
about.fields: pass: the reference verdict. fails: the numbers of the properties it fails (1 Significant, 2 Whole, 3 Established, 4 Grounded, 5 Self-contained, 6 Terms in full, 7 On the subject, 8 Faithful). borderline: true when a careful reader could decide the other way; score the judge with and without these. note: why.
about.caveats: One labeller. Not blind: the judge's eight failures of the last round were known when labelling. A later acronym written alone after its full form was given earlier in the same fact ('virtual reality (VR) system ... a VR system') is not counted as a failure.

1/S0/F0.note: Only expands the four acronyms, and is worded badly ('the abbreviations', 'respectively'), but introducing the terms is the goal of the segment and the brackets make the sentence clear.

1/S0/F1.note: A 120-word summary of the segment's motivating examples of what people associate with the terms; the lecturer raises each to ask whether it is XR, and teaches none of them. '3D or 4D' is not written in full. The one teachable point inside is the headset (sentences 59-61): worn on the head, blocks vision, the most common perception of VR.

1/S1/F0.note: The definition with what it is not, in one fact.

1/S1/F1.note: The lecturer teaches this reading of X on purpose (sentences 98-109).

1/S1/F2.note: Immersive experience and immersive technology are one point here; nothing added.

1/S2/F0.note: Sentences 125 and 126 state both extremes ('nothing virtual there', 'nothing real here'); sentence 127 only repeats them, so it need not be cited.

1/S2/F1.note: 'Intermediate state' paraphrases 'in between ... at one end we have augmented reality'; acceptable.

1/S2/F3.note: Keeps the limit 'in a broad sense'.

1/S3/F0.note: One list with all members and figures, year and the remark that the figures may be larger now. Market figures are what this segment is there to teach.

1/S3/F2.note: A split of the market study in F1 (no year or source of its own); could be one fact with F1, but can be asked about separately.

1/S3/F4.note: Rightly leaves out who made the word popular.

1/S3/F5.note: F6 is the detail of this fact's 'reimagines the way humans interact'; the two could be one point.

1/S5/F0.note: The lecturer says the paper is one of the earliest 'in this field' and shaped 'the area', meaning virtual and augmented reality. The fact names the nearest noun instead: 'the field of mixed reality visual displays', taken from the paper's title.

4/S0/F2.note: Folds the lecturer's comments (other stimuli possible, sights and sounds primary) into the dictionary definition; they are cited.

4/S1/F0.note: The list of the three characteristics, naming its members without describing them, which is what the extraction prompt asks for; F1, F3 and F4 each describe one member. Long, and its last clause (telling VR systems from others) could go. Not a summary of the segment.

4/S1/F3.note: 'this immersive experience' points at the experience named in the same sentence; the code check's flag is a false alarm.

4/S2/F3.note: Leaves out why it is partly immersive (it blocks the visual and partly the auditory sense, sentence 146); see missed.json.

16/S0/F0.note: With F1 this is one point, that tracking is an essential part of an XR system, split into two thin facts.

16/S0/F3.note: Turns 'AR requires virtual content to be registered' into 'tracking is primarily about registering'; the lecturer says AR tracking is more about tracking objects moving in the field of view. Close enough to pass.

16/S1/F3.note: One point about eye tracking (when it is needed, and that it may be part of head tracking). Splitting it gives two thin facts.

16/S1/F5.note: The lecturer says perfect matching 'may not be required'; the fact says it 'is not required'.

16/S1/F9.note: 'for this' points at the alerting named in the same sentence; the code check's flag is a false alarm.

16/S1/F11.note: 'this is generally classified' points at the live capture named in the same sentence; the code check's flag is a false alarm.

16/S2/F1.note: The list of the two kinds, by name; F2 and F5 define them.

16/S2/F3.note: The lecturer says outside-in tracking is used by most VR headsets today. The fact says most VR headsets that use external sensors fall under outside-in tracking, which is true by definition and loses the point.

16/S3/F0.note: Sentences 102-103 recap the previous segment ('we have seen ... there are two ways'); the fact restates the recap and adds nothing (the same point is 16/S2/F1).
